chapters.title: Sacrifice and Offering
chapters.subtitle: In the Bible an offering is first a gift that brings you near to God, often shared as a meal
chapters.trueMeaning: A gift that brings you near
chapters.nutshell: In English, “sacrifice” usually means giving up something painful or a death. The main Hebrew word, *qorban*, comes from a root meaning “to come near”: an offering is something you bring close to God so that you can come close too. Many offerings were gifts, shared meals, or ways of cleansing God's dwelling, and after the Temple fell, prayer, praise and kindness were called offerings.
chapters.bigIdea: Biblical sacrifice is about drawing near to God with a gift, sharing his table and being made clean, and the New Testament turns this language into a whole life offered to God in Jesus.
skeleton: In English, sacrifice sounds like loss, pain and death
Qorban: an offering is something “brought near”
Olah, zevach, shelamim, minchah: smoke going up, a shared meal, a gift
Chatat and asham: cleansing God's dwelling and repairing wrongs
Drink offerings, contributions, the daily offering and the pleasing aroma
The Septuagint carried these words into Greek: thysia, prosphora, dōron, hilastērion
Translators chose words like “sin offering” and “propitiation” for good reasons, but some pictures were lost
Jesus and the apostles use this language for his self-giving and for our whole lives

sections.h: The English word and what we assume
p: Today the word **sacrifice** usually means losing something. Parents “sacrifice” for their children, a soldier “makes the ultimate sacrifice”, a chess player “sacrifices” a piece. So when we read about sacrifices in the Bible, many of us picture only an animal being killed and God being satisfied by its death.

The Hebrew words paint a wider picture. Most of them speak of **coming near**, **going up**, a **gift**, a **meal** or **cleansing**. Killing an animal was often part of the process, but it was not the centre of the meaning. To understand the Bible's language of offering, we need to hear these words as an Israelite family on its way to the Temple would have heard them.

sections.h: Qorban: what you bring near
p: The general Hebrew word for an offering is *qorban* (קָרְבָּן). It comes from the root *qarav* (קָרַב), “to come near, approach”. In its causative form, *hiqriv* (הִקְרִיב), the verb means “to bring near”, and that is the normal verb for offering. Leviticus begins: “When any one of you **brings an offering** to the LORD…” (Leviticus 1:2), literally “when a person brings near a near-thing”.

So the picture is not first of loss but of **approach**. The worshipper brings something close to God's dwelling, and in doing so comes close himself. The word appears in the Gospels too: Jesus mentions people who say of their goods, “It is *Corban*” (that is, given to God), and so refuse to help their parents (Mark 7:11). Jesus criticises a gift to God that becomes an excuse to neglect people.

sections.h: Smoke going up, a meal and a gift
p: The *olah* (עֹלָה) comes from *alah* (עָלָה), “to go up”. It was the offering that was **wholly burned** on the altar, so that all of it went up to God in smoke (Leviticus 1:9; Genesis 22:2). It expressed complete dedication.

The *zevach* (זֶבַח) comes from *zavach*, “to slaughter”, and the altar is a *mizbeach* (מִזְבֵּחַ), “place of slaughter”. But a *zevach* was usually a **meal**: a little was burned, a portion went to the priest, and the family ate the rest before the LORD. Elkanah shared portions with his family at Shiloh (1 Samuel 1:4–5), and Passover is called “the sacrifice (*zevach*) of the LORD's Passover” (Exodus 12:27). The most common meal-offering was the *shelamim* (שְׁלָמִים), from the same root as *shalom*: wholeness, peace, well-being (Leviticus 3). Its meat had to be eaten soon, at a joyful feast (Leviticus 7:15; Deuteronomy 12:7).

The *minchah* (מִנְחָה) simply means **gift** or **tribute**. Jacob sends a *minchah* to Esau (Genesis 32:13), and Ehud brings tribute to a king (Judges 3:15). In Leviticus 2 it is the grain offering of flour, oil and incense. Cain and Abel each bring a *minchah* (Genesis 4:3–4).

sections.h: Cleansing, repairing and everyday offerings
p: The *chatat* (חַטָּאת) is spelled like the word for “sin”, so it is traditionally called the **sin offering**. Many scholars today prefer “**purification offering**”, because its blood was applied to the altar and the sanctuary to cleanse them (Leviticus 16:16), and it was brought even where no moral wrong had been done, such as after childbirth (Leviticus 12:6). It dealt with the impurity of sin and death that spoils the place where God lives among his people.

The *asham* (אָשָׁם) means guilt or **reparation**. The worshipper who had wronged God or a neighbour first paid back what he owed, plus a fifth, and then brought the *asham* (Leviticus 5:15–16; 6:5). Repair came before ritual. Isaiah uses this word for the Servant: “when his soul makes an *asham*” (Isaiah 53:10).

The *nesekh* (נֶסֶךְ) was a **drink offering** of wine poured out at the altar alongside other offerings (Numbers 15:5; 28:7). Jacob poured one on a stone pillar (Genesis 35:14). The *terumah* (תְּרוּמָה) is a **contribution**, something lifted off and set aside from a larger amount for God. God tells Moses to receive a *terumah* for the Tabernacle “from every man whose heart moves him” (Exodus 25:2). The KJV calls it a “heave offering”.

The *tamid* (תָּמִיד), “continual”, was the **daily offering** of a lamb every morning and evening (Exodus 29:38–42; Numbers 28:3–6). It kept the rhythm of Israel's day. Many offerings are called a *reach nichoach* (רֵיחַ נִיחוֹחַ), “a soothing, restful aroma” (Genesis 8:21; Leviticus 1:9). The word *nichoach* is related to *nuach*, “to rest”. It is the language of a guest's gift that pleases the host, not of an angry god being bought off.

sections.h: The Greek words and the Septuagint
p: When Jews translated the Hebrew Bible into Greek (the Septuagint), they used *thysia* (θυσία) for many offerings, especially *zevach* and *minchah*. *Thysia* comes from *thuō*, “to sacrifice, slaughter”; Peter hears “Rise, kill (*thuson*) and eat” (Acts 10:13). The *olah* usually became *holokautōma* (ὁλοκαύτωμα), “wholly burnt”.

*Prosphora* (προσφορά), literally “a bringing toward”, is close to the idea of *qorban* (Ephesians 5:2; Hebrews 10:10). *Dōron* (δῶρον) means **gift**; Mark explains *Corban* as “*dōron*” (Mark 7:11). *Spendomai* (σπένδομαι), “to be poured out as a drink offering”, is Paul's picture for his own life (Philippians 2:17; 2 Timothy 4:6).

Most striking is *hilastērion* (ἱλαστήριον). In the Septuagint it translates *kapporet*, the gold **cover of the ark** where blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement (Exodus 25:17; Leviticus 16:14). Hebrews 9:5 uses it in that sense, and Paul says God put Jesus forward as a *hilastērion* (Romans 3:25).

sections.h: What translators miss — and why
p: English has no single word for *qorban*, so translators use “offering”, “sacrifice” and “oblation” (from the Latin Vulgate's *oblatio*). “Sacrifice” comes from Latin *sacrificium*, “making sacred”, but in modern English it has drifted toward **loss**. The Vulgate also called Romans 12:1 a living *hostia* (“victim”), the word that later gave English “host” for communion bread.

The KJV's “**meat offering**” for *minchah* (Leviticus 2) meant “food” in 1611; today it misleads, since the offering was grain, so modern versions say “grain offering”. For *shelamim*, the KJV says “peace offering”, the NIV “fellowship offering” and the NRSV “sacrifice of well-being”: each catches part of a word that means wholeness shared at a meal. “Sin offering” keeps the link with sin but hides the cleansing; “purification offering” shows the cleansing but hides the spelling link. The word “holocaust” (from *holokautōma*) once meant a burnt offering, which is one reason many Jews prefer the word **Shoah** for the murder of six million Jews.

For *hilastērion* in Romans 3:25, the KJV and ESV say “propitiation” (appeasing), the RSV “expiation” (removing sin), and the NIV and NRSV “sacrifice of atonement”. Translators disagree because the Greek word could carry several ideas. Some scholars point out that the Septuagint background suggests “**mercy seat**”, the place where God meets his people and cleanses them.

sections.h: The culture behind the words
p: Israel was a nation of farmers and shepherds. An offering was taken from what fed your family: the **firstborn** of the flock, the **firstfruits** of the harvest, flour, oil and wine. Bringing it meant trusting God to provide again. Families travelled to the Temple for the pilgrim feasts and ate their offerings together in God's presence. The command was: “there you shall eat before the LORD your God, and you shall **rejoice**” (Deuteronomy 12:7). In the ancient world, eating at someone's table meant friendship and covenant.

The prophets insisted that offerings without justice are empty: “to obey is better than sacrifice” (1 Samuel 15:22); “I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice” (Hosea 6:6); “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit” (Psalm 51:17). The Mishnah, after comparing large and small offerings, concludes: “whether one brings much or little, what matters is that he directs his heart to heaven” (Mishnah Menachot 13:11).

In the Greek and Roman cities of Paul's world, *thysia* was everywhere. Temples sacrificed to the gods, meat from those sacrifices was sold in the market, and people held banquets in temple dining rooms. That is why Paul discusses “food offered to idols” and eating “in an idol's temple” (1 Corinthians 8:10; 10:25–28). A sacrifice there also meant a meal and fellowship with a god.

sections.h: After the Temple: offerings of the lips
p: Even before the Temple fell, Scripture saw prayer as an offering: “Let my prayer be counted as incense before you, and the lifting up of my hands as the evening sacrifice (*minchah*)” (Psalm 141:2). Hosea told Israel to return to God saying, “we will pay with **bulls of our lips**” (Hosea 14:2, literal).

When the Romans destroyed the Temple in AD 70, the sacrifices stopped. Jewish tradition remembers Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai comforting a student at the ruins: we still have an atonement as great as this, **acts of loving-kindness**, “for I desire *chesed* and not sacrifice” (Avot de-Rabbi Natan 4, quoting Hosea 6:6). The Talmud teaches that the daily prayers were arranged to match the daily offerings (Berakhot 26b). To this day the Amidah is prayed at the times of the old *tamid*.

sections.h: Jesus and the apostles in context
p: Jesus took offerings seriously and put people first: “if you are offering your gift (*dōron*) at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift… First be reconciled to your brother” (Matthew 5:23–24). He twice quoted Hosea 6:6, “I desire mercy, and not sacrifice” (Matthew 9:13; 12:7). At his last Passover meal he spoke of “my blood of the covenant” (Mark 14:24), echoing the covenant meal at Sinai, where Israel offered peace offerings and then “ate and drank” before God (Exodus 24:5–11).

The apostles describe Jesus' self-giving with the full range of offering words: a Passover lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7), “a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God” (Ephesians 5:2), an offering made once for all (Hebrews 10:10), the place of mercy and cleansing (Romans 3:25). Then they apply the same words to believers: our bodies as “a living sacrifice” (Romans 12:1), praise as “the fruit of lips” (Hebrews 13:15), sharing with others (Hebrews 13:16) and gifts to mission (Philippians 4:18).

sections.h: Living it out
p: If an offering is a gift that brings you near, then worship is not about paying God off but about **coming close**. You come with what you have: time, money, work, prayer, praise, and the whole of your body and life (Romans 12:1). You come joyfully, as a guest invited to a meal.
> The question is not “What must I lose?” but “What can I bring near to God, and whom can I bring with me?”

Like the *asham*, offering also means putting things right with people first. Like the *tamid*, it means a steady rhythm of morning and evening prayer. And like the shared *shelamim*, it means eating and rejoicing together, making room at the table for the poor, the stranger and the widow (Deuteronomy 16:11).

quiz.q: What does the root of qorban mean?
quiz.why: Qorban comes from qarav, “to come near”; an offering is what is brought near to God.

quiz.q: What happened to most of a zevach or shelamim offering?
options: It was eaten by the worshippers as a meal
It was sold in the market
quiz.why: Only part was burned and part went to the priest; the family ate the rest joyfully before the LORD.

quiz.q: Why did the KJV call the minchah a “meat offering”?
options: It was a mistake in the Hebrew
quiz.why: Old English “meat” meant food in general; the minchah was usually grain, flour and oil.

quiz.q: In the Septuagint, what does hilastērion (Romans 3:25) translate?
options: The kapporet, the cover of the ark (mercy seat)
quiz.why: The Septuagint uses hilastērion for the kapporet, and Hebrews 9:5 uses it for the mercy seat.

quiz.q: Which verse speaks of paying “bulls of our lips”, praise instead of animals?
quiz.why: Hosea 14:2 pictures returning to God with words of prayer as an offering; Hebrews 13:15 echoes it.

chapters.title: Word
chapters.subtitle: In Hebrew a word is not just a sound or a letter on a page; it is something that happens
chapters.trueMeaning: Speech that acts: word, thing, event
chapters.nutshell: In English a “word” is a small unit of language. The Hebrew *davar* means a word, but also a thing, a matter and an event: when God speaks, things happen. The Greek *logos* adds the ideas of message, account and reason, and John uses it to say that God's creating, saving Word became a human being in Jesus.
chapters.bigIdea: God's word in Scripture is living speech that creates, acts and comes true, and in Jesus that word took flesh and lived among us.
skeleton: In English a word is small, cheap and easily forgotten
Davar means word, thing and event together: God's speech acts
Amar, imrah and the “Ten Words”: what God says and what he gives
In the Aramaic Targums, “the Memra (Word) of the LORD” acts in the world
Greek logos and rhēma both mean word, and both translate davar
The popular logos/rhēma distinction does not hold up in the texts
John's “Word” draws on Genesis, Jewish wisdom and Greek thought together
Living by every word that comes from God's mouth means hearing and doing

sections.h: The English word and what we assume
p: We use the English word **word** in many small ways: a word in a dictionary, a word on a page, “just words”. We even say “talk is cheap” and “actions speak louder than words”. So when we read “the word of God”, many of us think only of a printed book, or of information about God.

The Hebrew Bible thinks differently. A word is **an act**. Once spoken, it goes out and does things. God speaks and the world exists; a father's blessing cannot be taken back; a prophet's word comes true. To read “word” in the Bible well, we need to hear it with Hebrew ears.

sections.h: Davar: word, thing and event
p: The main Hebrew word is *davar* (דָּבָר), used well over a thousand times. It means **word** or **speech**, but just as often **thing**, **matter** or **event**. Genesis 22:1 begins “After these *devarim*”, which translators render “after these things”. The book of Chronicles is called in Hebrew *Divrei HaYamim*, “the words (events) of the days”, and Solomon's deeds are recorded in “the book of the *divrei* of Solomon” (1 Kings 11:41). Even modern Hebrew says *ein davar*, “it's nothing”, literally “there is no thing”.

So for a Hebrew speaker, a word and the thing it brings about belong together. “By the **word** of the LORD the heavens were made… For he spoke, and it came to be” (Psalm 33:6, 9). God's word “shall not return to me empty, but it shall accomplish that which I purpose” (Isaiah 55:11). He “sent out his word and healed them” (Psalm 107:20). God's word is like “fire” and like “a hammer that breaks the rock in pieces” (Jeremiah 23:29).

The verb is *dibber* (דִּבֶּר), “to speak”. “God **spoke** all these words” (Exodus 20:1). Again and again the prophets say, “The word of the LORD came to…” (Genesis 15:1; Jeremiah 1:2), as if the word were something that arrives and acts.

sections.h: Amar, imrah and the Ten Words
p: A second verb is *amar* (אָמַר), “to say”. Creation happens through it: “And God **said**, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light” (Genesis 1:3). The Mishnah counts the times God “said” in Genesis 1 and teaches that “with ten utterances the world was created” (Mishnah Avot 5:1). From *amar* comes *imrah* (אִמְרָה), “saying, word”, used often in Psalm 119: “I have stored up your **word** in my heart, that I might not sin against you” (Psalm 119:11).

What we call the Ten Commandments the Hebrew Bible calls *aseret ha-devarim* (עֲשֶׂרֶת הַדְּבָרִים), “**the Ten Words**” (Exodus 34:28; Deuteronomy 4:13; 10:4). The Greek translation made this “ten words”, and that is where the name **Decalogue** comes from. Jewish tradition still calls them “the Ten Utterances”. The first “word” is not a command at all but a statement of grace: “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (Exodus 20:2).

sections.h: Memra: the Word of the LORD in the Targums
p: In synagogues in Jesus' time and after, the Hebrew Scriptures were translated aloud into Aramaic, the people's everyday language. These translations, later written down, are called the **Targums**. Where the Hebrew says that God himself acts or is present, the Targums often say “**the Memra (Word) of the LORD**”. In Targum Onkelos, for example, Adam and Eve hear “the voice of the Memra of the LORD God” (Genesis 3:8), and Moses brings Israel out “to meet the Memra of the LORD” (Exodus 19:17).

Scholars debate what the Memra means. Many see it as a reverent way of speaking about God's action without describing God too directly; others see something closer to a distinct figure. The Targums were written down later than the New Testament, though their oral practice is older. So we should say carefully: some scholars compare the Memra with John's “Word”, as one more sign that John's language was at home in the Jewish world.

sections.h: The Greek words: logos and rhēma
p: The Septuagint translates *davar* mainly with two Greek words. *Logos* (λόγος), from *legō*, “to say”, means word, statement, message, account, reckoning and reason. A master “settles **accounts** (*logos*)” with his servants (Matthew 18:23); we must all give an “**account**” to God (Hebrews 4:13). Luke calls his first book a *logos* (Acts 1:1).

*Rhēma* (ῥῆμα) means “what is spoken”: a word, a saying, and, just like *davar*, a **matter** or **event**. The shepherds say, “Let us go and see this *rhēma* that has happened” (Luke 2:15). The angel tells Mary that “no *rhēma* will be impossible with God” (Luke 1:37), echoing the Septuagint of Genesis 18:14: “Is any *rhēma* too hard for the Lord?” Behind both Greek words stands the Hebrew *davar*: a word that becomes a thing.

sections.h: A popular distinction that does not hold
p: You may have heard that *logos* means the general, written word of God, while *rhēma* is a special, personal word God speaks to you today. This idea is popular, but **the texts do not support it**. Both words are used for spoken and written words, for Scripture, for Jesus' teaching and for the gospel message.

Jesus calls his spoken teaching both “these **logoi** of mine” (Matthew 7:24) and “the **rhēmata** I have spoken to you” (John 6:63). Peter calls the gospel “the living and abiding **logos** of God” and two verses later “the **rhēma** of the Lord [that] remains forever… this **rhēma** is the good news that was preached to you” (1 Peter 1:23–25), using both words for the same thing. Hebrews says the **logos** of God is “living and active” (Hebrews 4:12). The difference between the words is mostly one of style, not of two kinds of revelation.

sections.h: What translators miss — and why
p: Because *davar* means both “word” and “thing”, translators must choose in every verse. They write “after these **things**” in Genesis 22:1 (KJV, ESV) or simply “some time later” (NIV). That is right for English, but readers lose the sense that events are God's words being fulfilled. In the same way, “Ten **Commandments**” (KJV, ESV, NIV in Exodus 34:28) is a fair summary, but it hides “Ten **Words**” and the gracious first word.

In Luke 1:37 the KJV and ESV say “with God nothing shall be impossible”, while the NIV has “no word from God will ever fail”. Both are possible, because *rhēma* means both word and thing. In Romans 10:17 the KJV says “hearing by the word of God”, following later Greek manuscripts, while the ESV and NIV follow older ones that read “word of Christ”: a textual choice, not a theological trick.

For John 1:1 the Latin Vulgate wrote *Verbum*, “word”, and English followed with “the Word”. In the sixteenth century the scholar Erasmus preferred the Latin *sermo*, “speech, discourse”, closer to living speech, which caused controversy. Some Chinese Bibles chose *Dao*, “the Way”. Every choice catches part of *logos*: word, speech, message, reason. English “Word” is kept because no other single word does better, but we must fill it with its Hebrew weight.

sections.h: The culture behind the words
p: Israel was mainly an **oral culture**. Few people owned books; agreements, blessings, vows and testimony were spoken. Once Isaac had blessed Jacob, he could not take it back (Genesis 27:33–35). A person who made a vow “shall not break his **word** (*davar*)” (Numbers 30:2). In court, the spoken word of two or three witnesses decided a case. Words had weight because people lived by them.

In the Greek world, *logos* was also a word of **philosophers**. Around 500 BC Heraclitus spoke of the *logos* as the reason that orders the universe, and the Stoics later taught that a divine *logos* runs through all things. The Jewish thinker Philo of Alexandria used *logos* for God's agent in creation. At the same time, Jewish wisdom writings pictured God's Wisdom beside him at creation (Proverbs 8:22–31) and said God “made all things by your **word**” (Wisdom of Solomon 9:1). Wisdom was even told to “pitch your tent in Jacob” (Sirach 24:8).

John wrote into both worlds. A Greek reader heard “the Logos” and thought of the reason behind the world; a Jewish reader heard “In the beginning” and thought of Genesis, of God's creating word and of Wisdom dwelling in Israel. Most scholars see the Jewish Scriptures as John's main background.

sections.h: Jesus and the apostles: the Word became flesh
p: John opens his Gospel with the opening words of Genesis: “**In the beginning** was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God… All things were made through him” (John 1:1–3). Then he says something no philosopher expected: “the Word **became flesh** and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). The verb means “pitched his tent”, recalling the Tabernacle and Wisdom dwelling in Jacob. God's creating, saving *davar* became a human life you could see and touch (1 John 1:1).

Jesus' own words act like God's *davar*. The centurion says, “only say the **word**, and my servant will be healed” (Matthew 8:8). Jesus answers temptation with Deuteronomy: “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every **word** that comes from the mouth of God” (Matthew 4:4). His followers say, “You have the **words** of eternal life” (John 6:68). And Revelation names the returning King: “his name is called **The Word of God**” (Revelation 19:13).

sections.h: Living it out
p: If God's word is a *davar*, then reading Scripture is not only gathering information. It is letting God's speech **do something** in us: create, heal, correct and send. Psalm 119 does not say “your word is a library” but “a **lamp to my feet**” (Psalm 119:105): light for the next step.
> In Hebrew a word is not finished until it happens. God's word is finished in us when we do it.

It also means our own words matter. Speak promises you will keep, blessings that build up, and truth that heals. Jesus said that whoever hears his words and **does** them is like a man who built his house on the rock (Matthew 7:24).

chapters.title: Scripture and Voice
chapters.subtitle: The Bible was first something read aloud and heard, the voice of God to be obeyed
chapters.trueMeaning: What is read aloud, heard and obeyed
chapters.nutshell: “Scripture” means “writing”, and we usually meet the Bible silently, on a page or a screen. Jews call the Bible *Miqra*, “what is read aloud”, and its heart is *qol*, a voice, and *shema*, hearing that becomes obeying. The Greek *graphē* (writing) is the same Scripture: God-breathed words meant to be read aloud to God's people and lived.
chapters.bigIdea: Scripture is God's voice written down so that it can be read aloud, heard together and obeyed.
skeleton: We meet the Bible mostly as a silent book

sections.h: The English word and what we assume
p: The English word **Scripture** comes from the Latin *scriptura*, “writing”. The word **Bible** comes from the Greek *biblia*, “books” or “scrolls”. Most of us meet the Bible as a book we read silently, alone, perhaps on a phone. So we tend to think of it as a text to study, a book of information about God.

But for most of history, God's people did not own Bibles. They **heard** them. In the synagogue and in the early church, Scripture was read aloud, often memorised, and received together as the **voice** of God. The Hebrew and Greek words carry that sound.

sections.h: Miqra: what is read aloud
p: One Jewish name for the Bible is *Miqra* (מִקְרָא). It comes from *qara* (קָרָא), “to call out, proclaim, read aloud”. When Ezra read the Torah to the people, the Levites “gave the sense, so that the people understood the **reading** (*miqra*)” (Nehemiah 8:8). The same word describes the festivals as a “holy **convocation**”, a *miqra qodesh*, a day when people are called together (Leviticus 23:2–3).

So the very name of Scripture tells us how it was used: **called out** to a gathered people. Later the Mishnah describes Jewish education: “At five years old, *Miqra* (Scripture); at ten, Mishnah…” (Mishnah Avot 5:21). Children learned the Bible first by hearing and reciting it.

sections.h: Tanakh, and “it is written”
p: Jews call the Hebrew Bible the **Tanakh** (תַּנַ"ךְ), from the first letters of its three parts: *Torah* (תּוֹרָה), the instruction of the five books of Moses; *Nevi'im* (נְבִיאִים), the Prophets; and *Ketuvim* (כְּתוּבִים), the Writings, such as Psalms, Proverbs and Daniel. It contains the same books as the Protestant Old Testament, in a different order, usually ending with Chronicles. Jesus speaks of “the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms” (Luke 24:44). Many scholars think his phrase “from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah” (Luke 11:51) runs from the first to the last murder in that order (Genesis 4; 2 Chronicles 24:20–22).

*Ketuvim* comes from *katav*, “to write”. The word *katuv* (כָּתוּב) means “written”, and *kakatuv*, “**as it is written**”, introduces Scripture as the final authority (2 Kings 14:6). Yet even the written Torah was meant for the mouth: “This Book of the Law shall not depart from your **mouth**, but you shall meditate on it day and night” (Joshua 1:8). The verb for meditate, *hagah*, means to murmur: reading half aloud.

sections.h: Qol: a voice, not an image
p: *Qol* (קוֹל) means **voice** or **sound**. In the garden, Adam and Eve “heard the *qol* of the LORD God walking” (Genesis 3:8), which can mean his voice or simply the sound of his steps. At Sinai the *qolot*, “voices”, were thunderings, and Hebrew says strikingly that “all the people **saw** the *qolot*” (Exodus 20:18). Moses later reminds Israel: “You heard the sound of words, but saw no form; there was only a **voice**” (Deuteronomy 4:12). Israel's faith rests on hearing God, not on seeing an image of him.

Psalm 29 repeats “the *qol* of the LORD” seven times: it thunders over the waters, breaks cedars and shakes the wilderness. Yet to Elijah, God came not in wind, earthquake or fire but in a *qol demamah daqqah* (1 Kings 19:12), literally “a voice (sound) of thin silence”.

Later rabbis spoke of the *bat qol* (בַּת קוֹל), literally “daughter of a voice”, an echo or voice from heaven. The Talmud says that after the last prophets died, Israel still received the *bat qol* (Yoma 9b). In a famous story, the rabbis even refused to settle a law by a heavenly voice, quoting “It is not in heaven” (Deuteronomy 30:12; Bava Metzia 59b): God had given the Torah to be studied and applied on earth.

sections.h: Shema: to hear is to obey
p: The central confession of Israel begins with one word: “*Shema* (שְׁמַע), **Hear**, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4). The verb *shama* (שָׁמַע) means to hear, to listen, to understand and **to obey**. Biblical Hebrew has no common separate word for “obey”; real hearing shows itself in doing. God tells Abraham, “because you have **obeyed** my voice” (Genesis 22:18), literally “because you **heard** my voice”.

At Sinai Israel answers, *na'aseh ve-nishma*, “All that the LORD has spoken **we will do, and we will hear**” (Exodus 24:7). Jewish tradition loves the order: doing comes first, and deeper hearing follows. Psalm 95 pleads, “Today, if you **hear** his voice, do not harden your hearts” (Psalm 95:7–8), a warning Hebrews repeats to Christians (Hebrews 3:7–8).

sections.h: The Greek words: written, God-breathed, read aloud
p: *Graphē* (γραφή) means “writing”, but in the New Testament it always means **Scripture**, the Jewish Scriptures. The Bereans “examined the Scriptures daily” to test Paul's message (Acts 17:11). *Gramma* (γράμμα) is a **letter** of the alphabet or a document; people wondered how Jesus knew “letters” without having studied (John 7:15). Paul says “the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3:6), contrasting the law on stone tablets with the Spirit writing on hearts (3:3, 7), not literal with “spiritual” reading.

Paul tells Timothy that from childhood he has known “the sacred writings” (2 Timothy 3:15), and “All Scripture is **breathed out by God** (*theopneustos*) and profitable for teaching” (3:16). The word, found only here, joins *theos* (God) and *pneō* (breathe). Peter says the prophets spoke “carried along by the Holy Spirit” (2 Peter 1:21), using the verb for a ship driven by the wind (Acts 27:15).

Jesus answers the tempter, *gegraptai* (γέγραπται), “**It is written**” (Matthew 4:4, 7, 10). The tense means “it has been written and still stands”. *Phōnē* (φωνή) is “voice”: a voice from heaven at Jesus' baptism (Mark 1:11), and “My sheep **hear my voice**” (John 10:27). And *anaginōskō* (ἀναγινώσκω) means “to **read aloud**”: Jesus “stood up to read” in Nazareth (Luke 4:16), and Revelation blesses “the one who reads aloud… and those who hear” (Revelation 1:3).

sections.h: What translators miss — and why
p: In 1 Kings 19:12 the KJV gave us the beloved “a **still small voice**”. The NIV has “a gentle whisper”, the ESV “the sound of a low whisper”, and the NRSV “a sound of sheer silence”. The Hebrew *demamah* means stillness or silence and *daqqah* means thin or fine, so translators must choose between a quiet voice and an almost silent sound. Each is defensible; the Hebrew holds the paradox of a voice made of silence.

Because *shama* means both hear and obey, the KJV often writes “hearken” or “obey” (“will we do, and be obedient”, Exodus 24:7). That is correct English, but readers lose that **hearing and obeying are one word**. In 2 Timothy 3:16 the KJV's “given by **inspiration** of God” comes through the Latin Vulgate's *divinitus inspirata*, “breathed into”. The NIV's “God-breathed” is closer to the Greek: Scripture breathed out by God, like the breath that gave Adam life (Genesis 2:7).

In 2 Corinthians 3:6 the KJV prints “the letter killeth, but the **spirit** giveth life” with a small “s”, which encouraged reading it as “literal versus spiritual meaning”. Modern versions such as the ESV and NIV capitalise “Spirit”, since Paul is speaking of the Holy Spirit. Finally, the name “Old Testament” is a Christian title; Jews speak of Tanakh or Miqra. Christians are not wrong to use it, but the Jewish names remind us that these books were already Scripture, read aloud, before the New Testament was written.

sections.h: The culture behind the words
p: Scripture was written by trained scribes on long **scrolls** of leather or papyrus. Scrolls were costly, so most people never owned one. Jeremiah dictated his words to Baruch, who wrote them on a scroll and **read it aloud** in the Temple (Jeremiah 36:4–10). Synagogues kept scrolls and read them every Sabbath: “Moses has been read every Sabbath in the synagogues” (Acts 15:21). After the Torah reading came a reading from the Prophets, later called the *Haftarah*, and often a sermon (Acts 13:15). In later centuries the whole Torah was read through in a fixed cycle.

Learning was largely **oral**. Students memorised long passages, recited them and discussed them together. Later Jewish scribes added marks to the Hebrew text showing how each verse should be **chanted**, and the Torah is still sung aloud in synagogues today. Reading itself was usually aloud: Philip “heard” the Ethiopian official reading Isaiah in his chariot (Acts 8:30).

The Greco-Roman world worked the same way. Letters were carried by messengers and read aloud to their hearers. Paul asks that his letters be **read to all** the believers and passed between churches (Colossians 4:16; 1 Thessalonians 5:27), and tells Timothy to devote himself “to the public reading of Scripture” (1 Timothy 4:13). The first Christians received the Bible as **listeners in a congregation**.

sections.h: Jesus and the apostles in context
p: Jesus grew up in this world of hearing. In Nazareth he stood in the synagogue, was handed the scroll of Isaiah, read aloud and then said, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled **in your hearing**” (Luke 4:16–21). He quoted Scripture from memory, “It is written”, and he asked his opponents, “Have you not read…?” (Matthew 12:3). After his resurrection “he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24:45).

His own voice became the voice to obey. At the transfiguration the heavenly voice said, “This is my beloved Son; **listen to him**” (Mark 9:7), the language of the Shema. When the voice spoke again, some in the crowd said, “It thundered” (John 12:28–29), just as *qol* can mean both voice and thunder. Jesus said, “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me” (John 10:27): hearing that leads to following.

sections.h: Living it out
p: Try to meet Scripture as it was meant to be met: **read it aloud**, listen to it, memorise it, talk about it at home and on the road (Deuteronomy 6:7). Read it with others, not only alone. Reading together protects us from making the Bible say only what we want.
> In the Bible, you have not really heard until you have obeyed.

And remember that Scripture is not only a book to master but a **voice to answer**. James warns, “be doers of the word, and not hearers only” (James 1:22). Each time you read, ask: what is God saying, and what will I do because I have heard it?

keyPoints: Miqra, a Jewish name for Scripture, means “what is read aloud”, from qara, to call out.
The Tanakh has three parts: Torah, Prophets and Writings, the same books as the Protestant Old Testament in a different order.
Israel's faith began with a voice (qol), not an image (Deuteronomy 4:12).
Shema means hear and obey: real hearing shows itself in doing (Exodus 24:7).
Graphē is God-breathed writing (2 Timothy 3:16), and in the ancient world it was read aloud to congregations.
Translations like “still small voice”, “inspiration” and “the spirit giveth life” each catch part of the original.
Jesus read Scripture aloud, quoted it from memory, and calls his followers to hear his voice and follow.
reflect: When did you last read Scripture aloud or hear it read with others? What difference might that make?
Is there something you have “heard” from Scripture but not yet obeyed?
How can you help a child or a new believer to hear, memorise and live God's word?

quiz.q: What does the Hebrew name Miqra say about Scripture?
options: It is what is read aloud
quiz.why: Miqra comes from qara, to call out or read aloud; Scripture was read to the gathered people.

quiz.q: What are the three parts of the Tanakh?
quiz.why: Tanakh is an acronym of Torah, Nevi'im (Prophets) and Ketuvim (Writings).

quiz.q: What does the Hebrew verb shama include?
quiz.why: Shama means to hear, listen and obey; Genesis 22:18 says Abraham “heard” (obeyed) God's voice.

quiz.q: What does theopneustos (2 Timothy 3:16) literally mean?
quiz.why: It joins theos (God) and pneō (breathe): Scripture is breathed out by God.

quiz.q: Why did the KJV's small “s” in 2 Corinthians 3:6 matter?
options: It encouraged a “literal versus spiritual reading” idea, though Paul means the Holy Spirit
It made the verse about angels
quiz.why: Greek had no capitals; modern versions write “Spirit” because Paul contrasts the law on stone with the Holy Spirit.

terms.def: “What is read aloud”; a Jewish name for the Hebrew Bible.
The Hebrew Bible, named from its three parts: Torah, Nevi'im, Ketuvim.
Voice, sound or thunder; God's voice in Scripture.
In rabbinic writings, a voice or echo from heaven.
“Hear!”; to hear and obey; also the name of Israel's central confession (Deuteronomy 6:4).
“God-breathed”, Paul's description of Scripture in 2 Timothy 3:16.
The reading from the Prophets that follows the Torah reading in the synagogue.
